summary: Bolivia sorts passports into three groups: Group 1 — most of the EU, the UK, the United States, most of the Americas and a number of others — enters visa-free for up to 90 days a year; Group 2 pays for a tourist visa, obtainable on arrival or at a consulate; Group 3 needs a consular visa, issued after prior authorization from the Bolivian authorities.

fee.notes: 300 UFV (Bolivia's inflation-indexed unit of account; about Bs 1,005 at the UFV value of Bs 3.35 on 2 October 2026, so the boliviano amount rises over time). Paid into the Ministry of Government's fiscal account at Banco Unión once the migration officer has authorised the payment.

visaTypes.name: Consular Tourist Visa with prior authorization (Group 3)

source.name: Dirección General de Migración de Bolivia

fee.notes: 250 UFV for a stay of up to 30 days (about Bs 838 at the UFV value of Bs 3.35 on 2 October 2026). The Migration Directorate lists this tourist stay procedure for every nationality; a tourist visa entitles its holder to two such periods, within 90 days a year.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración — Trámites para extranjeros (Permanencia transitoria por turismo o visita)

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months on arrival. Bolivian officials are strict about damaged passports and about visa pages being intact.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración — Trámites para extranjeros (Permanencia transitoria por turismo o visita)

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required if you arrive from or have transited a country with risk of transmission. Bolivia's Migration Directorate also lists a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate among the requirements for a tourist visa or stay permit if you will visit high-risk endemic areas. Vaccination is strongly recommended — and sometimes checked on domestic flights — before traveling to the lowland departments of Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando, Tarija or the Yungas.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración — Autorización de Ingreso por Turismo o Visita (tourist visa requirements, cost and processing)

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry condition, but high-altitude medical care and evacuation from the Salar de Uyuni or the Amazon are expensive — cover that explicitly includes altitudes above 4,000 m is worth checking for.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración de Bolivia

onwardTicket.text: Group 2 tourist-visa applicants must show a travel itinerary or return ticket, an invitation from a person legally resident in Bolivia registered with the Migration Directorate, or a hotel booking. Airlines may also check for an onward ticket at check-in.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración — Autorización de Ingreso por Turismo o Visita (tourist visa requirements, cost and processing)

proofOfFunds.text: Group 2 tourist-visa applicants must prove economic solvency with a sworn declaration backed by documents, such as recent bank statements. No minimum sum is published, and none is set for visa-free visitors.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración — Autorización de Ingreso por Turismo o Visita (tourist visa requirements, cost and processing)

declarations.name: Customs declaration
declarations.text: Before entering or leaving Bolivia, travelers fill in customs Form 250, a sworn declaration of new goods carried in accompanied baggage (on entry) and of currency (on entry and exit). It is available pre-printed or electronically.

source.name: Aduana Nacional de Bolivia — Declaración de equipaje y divisas (Form. 250)

currencyLimits.text: Currency between USD 10,000 and USD 50,000 must be declared on entry, and between USD 10,000 and USD 20,000 on exit, on Form 250. Larger sums must be moved through a financial institution regulated by ASFI. Customs withholds 30% of undeclared currency, and of any amount above the limits.

source.name: Aduana Nacional de Bolivia — Declaración de equipaje y divisas (Form. 250)

notes: Coca leaf is legal to buy and chew inside Bolivia but exporting it is illegal almost everywhere else — do not carry it across the border.
Drone use near government buildings and in some national parks needs permission; equipment can be held at customs.
Archaeological items and textiles of cultural value cannot be exported without a permit from the culture ministry.

payments.text: Cash in bolivianos is essential outside La Paz, Santa Cruz and Sucre. Cards work in city hotels and better restaurants, but ATMs run dry in small towns and on the Uyuni circuit; dollar shortages in recent years have also made card and ATM access unreliable, so carry more cash than you think you need.

safety.text: Bolivia is not a violent-crime destination for most visitors, but three things need care: altitude, road travel, and political blockades (bloqueos) that can close highways and airports at short notice. Express kidnapping and fake-police scams occur in La Paz and Santa Cruz. Use only radio taxis booked through your hotel.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Bolivia travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to October is the dry season: clear skies over the Altiplano, reliable roads and the best conditions for Uyuni's mirror effect fading into hard white salt. December to March brings rain, which floods the salt flat for the mirror photographs but makes overland travel harder.

tips.text: El Alto airport serving La Paz sits at about 4,050 m — you land straight into thin air. Plan a slow first day, avoid alcohol, and consider arriving via Santa Cruz (400 m) or Sucre (2,800 m) if you are sensitive to altitude.

Many tour payments are in cash US dollars, and notes that are torn, written on or even slightly damaged are often refused. Bring pristine bills in small denominations. Migration fees are set in UFV and paid at Banco Unión, not in cash at the counter.
Bolivia runs on 230 V almost everywhere, but La Paz and parts of the Altiplano are on 115 V. Check the socket before plugging in anything without a dual-voltage adapter.

Road blockades over fuel, politics or mining are a normal feature of Bolivian life and can strand travelers for days. Build slack into overland itineraries and check local news before long bus journeys.
The visa-free allowance is 90 days within a calendar year, not per entry. Leaving and coming back does not reset it, and overstays are fined per day on departure.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bolivia?
faq.answer: It depends on which of Bolivia's three groups your passport falls into. Group 1 — most EU and Schengen states, the UK, the United States, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Israel, Turkey, Russia, Australia, New Zealand and most of Latin America — needs no visa and gets up to 90 days a year. Group 2 pays for a tourist visa that can be issued on arrival or at a consulate. Group 3 needs prior authorization from Bolivia before a consulate can issue a visa.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Bolivia?
faq.answer: No. Since Supreme Decree 5497 of 1 December 2025, US passport holders are in Group 1 and no longer need a consular visa or entry authorization to visit Bolivia as tourists — the former USD 160 visa no longer applies. Stays count toward the 90-day annual limit for visa-free visitors.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Bolivia?
faq.answer: Ninety days within a calendar year for visa-free visitors. Entry stamps often give 30 days initially. Check what you were granted and request more time, up to the 90-day annual cap, at a Dirección General de Migración office in any major city; the Directorate lists a fee of 250 UFV per period of up to 30 days.

faq.question: Can I really get a Bolivian visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Group 2 nationalities can, at La Paz (El Alto), Santa Cruz (Viru Viru) and the main land borders. Bring a passport valid for at least six months, a recent 4x4 cm photo on a white background, a travel itinerary or return ticket (or a registered invitation letter or hotel booking), documents backing a sworn statement of your funds, a yellow fever certificate if you will visit high-risk areas, and the fee of 300 UFV, paid at Banco Unión once the officer authorizes it. Processing takes about 10 to 30 minutes at the border. Applying at a consulate first is slower but avoids surprises at a remote border post.

faq.question: What is Group 3 and how long does it take?
faq.answer: Group 3 is a restricted list of nationalities for which the consulate cannot decide alone. The application is referred to the Bolivian authorities for prior authorization, which typically takes several weeks to a couple of months and often requires an invitation or sponsor. Group lists are revised by decree, so confirm your current status with a Bolivian consulate before making plans.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Bolivia?
faq.answer: It is required if you arrive from or have transited a yellow fever risk country, and Bolivia's Migration Directorate asks for a valid certificate with a tourist visa or stay application if you will visit high-risk endemic areas. Even if you are exempt, vaccination is strongly recommended before visiting the lowlands — Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando, Tarija and the Yungas — and is occasionally checked on domestic flights.
